headline: Space Force spends big. Startups strategize. Data becomes warfare.
deck: This week saw hefty contracts, strategic guidance for startups, and the weaponization of spatial data.

stories.head: Space Force hands SpaceX $4.16 billion contract
stories.body: The U.S. Space Force awarded SpaceX a substantial $4.16 billion to develop a satellite network for tracking airborne threats. This contract underscores the government's increasing reliance on private aerospace capabilities, as SpaceX continues to dominate the defense sector. With this deal, SpaceX solidifies its position as a key player in national security.
stories.soWhat: When the government spends this much on one player, it raises questions about competition and the future of smaller contractors.

stories.head: Space Force offers startups a playbook for defense contracts
stories.body: The Space Force's COMSO chief shared insights on securing defense contracts, emphasizing that charm and clarity can sometimes outweigh technical prowess. This guidance comes at a time when startups are scrambling for a foothold in the lucrative defense sector, especially as the FY27 budget earmarks an additional $1.4 billion for space resilience.
stories.soWhat: If charm is the new currency, we might see a wave of slick pitches that prioritize marketing over substance.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M amid defense pull-through
stories.body: True Anomaly secured $190 million in a Series C funding round, reaching a valuation of $1.6 billion. The company focuses on co-orbital security and space domain awareness, capitalizing on the Department of Defense's increasing interest in these capabilities. This funding reflects the broader trend of cash flow favoring companies with defense applications.
stories.soWhat: In space, it seems that the money is flowing toward security rather than exploration—perhaps a sign of the times.

watchlist.body: With a $4.16 billion contract in hand, all eyes will be on SpaceX's execution timeline and potential delays.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
